item.title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration from restricting mail-in ballots ahead of midterms
item.description: A federal judge in Boston blocked the USPS from enforcing Trump's executive order on mail-in voting rules ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Massachusetts on Tuesday blocked the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) from implementing part of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani granted a preliminary injunction preventing the USPS from implementing or enforcing Section 3 of Executive Order 14399 for the Nov. 3 midterm elections, or any earlier federal election.

The ruling prevents USPS from refusing to transmit mail-in or absentee ballots under the challenged section and blocks rulemaking to implement certain regulations outlined in the executive order for the November elections.

The injunction does not prevent the federal government from providing nonbinding USPS guidance on ballot-mail envelopes.

JUDGE HANDS TRUMP MAIL-BALLOT WIN FOR NOW AS DEMOCRATS’ NEXT MOVE LOOMS

Talwani held a hearing Friday on the plaintiffs' renewed request for a preliminary injunction. The Trump administration is expected to appeal Tuesday's ruling to the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston.

Trump signed the executive order in March as part of his election integrity agenda.

It directs the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to compile lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote and provide them to states, instructs the USPS to establish new standards for mail-in ballots, and directs the Department of Justice (DOJ) to prioritize investigations into state and local election officials who issue federal ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote.

"Cheating on mail-in voting is legendary. It’s horrible. Democrats want to use it for cheating," Trump said.

Tuesday's ruling comes weeks after the 1st Circuit rejected the administration's attempt to enforce other provisions of Trump's executive order while a separate legal challenge proceeds.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

In a 2-1 decision July 25, the appeals court denied the DOJ's request to pause a June ruling blocking several provisions of Trump's order in 23 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia.

That lawsuit was led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington. The states argued that the Constitution gives states primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that Trump exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements.

Talwani had previously blocked several provisions of the executive order in June, finding they likely exceeded the president's authority. The appeals court left that injunction in place July 25, while the administration's appeal proceeds.

The DOJ previously told the appeals court it could seek emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court if it did not prevail.

The League of Women Voters of Massachusetts praised Tuesday's ruling, saying it protects voting rights for people who rely on voting by mail.

"The League of Women Voters of Massachusetts commends the court for upholding one of our most sacred constitutional rights: the right to vote," a representative for the organization wrote in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "We are pleased to see this ruling and are committed to remaining in the fight to protect voting rights – not just for the Bay Staters who rely on mail voting, but for every American who utilizes this safe, secure, and trusted tool."

The White House, DOJ and USPS did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Talwani ordered the plaintiff organizations in Tuesday's ruling to post a nominal $100 bond by Aug. 18.

item.title: Taliban wipes out decades of progress as 2.4M Afghan girls remain locked out of school, UN agency says
item.description: UNESCO says 2.4 million Afghan girls are locked out of secondary school five years after the Taliban banned female education beyond the primary level.
item.content:encoded:
Five years after the Taliban reclaimed reclaimed Afghanistan, 2.4 million girls remain locked out of secondary school, wiping away decades of progress and leaving a generation of young women without access to the classroom.

Afghanistan is now the only country in the world that formally prohibits girls and women from receiving an education beyond the primary level, according to UNESCO, which issued a new call Tuesday for the "immediate and unconditional" restoration of their right to education.

The United Nations agency warned that the consequences of the Taliban's policies now reach far beyond the classroom, with women barred from most paid jobs and public-facing professions and facing restrictions on their ability to travel without a male guardian.

MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS

"Women have been erased from public life, and as a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark," UNESCO said in a statement.

The Taliban swept back into power on Aug. 15, 2021, as U.S. and NATO forces withdrew from Afghanistan after two decades of war.

The Taliban soon barred girls from secondary schools and later expanded the restrictions to universities, employment and other areas of public life.

Despite years of pressure from the United Nations, humanitarian groups, human rights advocates and several Islamic countries, the Taliban has refused to lift the education restrictions and has maintained that the issue is a domestic matter, according to The Associated Press.

IRAN AGREES NOT TO EXECUTE EIGHT WOMEN TIED TO ANTI-REGIME PROTESTS AFTER TRUMP'S PUBLIC APPEAL

The impact has been a dramatic reversal of the educational gains made by Afghan girls during the previous two decades.

While girls had severely limited access to schooling in 2001, nearly 1 million were enrolled in secondary education by 2021, according to UNESCO.

Five years later, an estimated 2.4 million girls are excluded from secondary education.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child's education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO's program coordinator for education in emergencies, said during a video news conference Tuesday, according to The AP. "It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

UNESCO warned that denying education to girls while restricting women's ability to work could deepen Afghanistan's already severe economic problems.

Nearly half of Afghanistan's population lives below the poverty line, according to UNESCO, which said preventing women from studying and working further limits their ability to support their families and contribute to the country's economy.

The agency also warned that excluding girls from school can damage their mental and physical well-being and increase the risk of early marriage.

The effects could also reach Afghan boys.

UNESCO said the Taliban's ban on female teachers teaching boys is worsening teacher shortages and undermining the quality of education across Afghanistan.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

With formal secondary and higher education closed to women and girls, UNESCO says it has turned to community-based education, literacy and skills development programs and psychosocial support to keep them learning.

Nearly 70,000 people have participated in UNESCO's programs, with women accounting for 73% of the learners, according to the agency.

Some literacy and skills classes take place in community spaces and in the homes of facilitators with the knowledge of authorities, according to The AP. More than 1,000 literacy facilitators are involved, most of whom have been trained by UNESCO and its partners.

UNESCO said a recent study found evidence that its literacy and skills programs have helped increase household incomes and improve livelihoods.

The agency acknowledged, however, that such efforts cannot replace formal schooling.

"Afghanistan's girls and women have the right to learn, to work, to move freely, and to shape their own futures," UNESCO said, adding that "the world must not look away until their human rights are restored."

UNESCO said it would continue working with local communities and partners to maintain alternative opportunities for Afghan women and girls while pressing for the education ban to be lifted.

"UNESCO continues to call for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls and women's right to secondary and higher education," Jaberian said Tuesday. "It is not negotiable. It's a basic human right and we reiterate that there is no substitute for this."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Tyler Feehan's mother and fiancée recall his excitement before fatal Middle East deployment
item.description: Army 1st Lt. Tyler Feehan's mother and fiancée reveal his excitement before the fatal Jordan drone attack and his resting place beside his grandfather, a Vietnam veteran.
item.content:encoded:
The grieving family of slain Army 1st Lt. Tyler Feehan remembered him as brave and passionate about life during an exclusive interview with "The Story" on Tuesday.

Feehan, a 25-year-old Army soldier from Georgia, was one of three U.S. service members killed in an Iranian drone attack at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 18.

"We are so proud of him, and it's just so touching that the country is also sharing in that pride with us," his mother Shari Feehan said.

In the emotional tribute, Feehan’s mother and fiancée shared details about his final resting place in Georgia and recalled how elated he was to be deployed to the Middle East.

TRUMP GIVES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO FALLEN ARMY LT TYLER FEEHAN AFTER FLYING GRIEVING FAMILY ON AIR FORCE ONE

"He was so excited to go," Feehan’s fiancée Claire Fletcher told Fox News. "He was just so excited to finally do his job that he's been training for and working towards, and he was so excited to get out there and make a difference and change lives."

While she was upset about her fiancé leaving on deployment, Fletcher said she was also excited for him to do what he loved and ultimately "come home."

US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM

"I was obviously very sad when I got the news that he was going to go, but I was very proud of him. I was like, ‘You know what, I just — I just want you to go out there. I want you to get the experience that you are wanting to get out of this, and to come home,'" Fletcher said.

"He was positive the entire time, and he was always like, ‘Oh yeah, I did so great today. We shot down 10 missiles,'" she added.

Feehan was assigned to the 2nd Battalion, 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

The Gold Star family told Fox News that military service is important to the Feehan family.

TRAVELERS UNITE IN POWERFUL MOMENT OF SILENCE AS FALLEN US SERVICE MEMBER RETURNS HOME

"He [Tyler] loved serving his country. His father did 26 years in the Army, and so the military and the country have always been very important to our family, and he carried that legacy on," Shari Feehan said.

The 25-year-old was laid to rest in Georgia on Friday, directly beside his grandfather, a Vietnam War veteran, who died a few days after the soldier’s tragic death in Jordan.

"Georgia National Cemetery, where Tyler is laid to rest with his grandfather, is just such a beautiful, peaceful place for our son," his mother told Fox News.

"They were together and very close in life, and now they can rest next to each other," she added.

Feehan’s mother also reflected on the family’s flight home to Georgia aboard Air Force One following an invitation from President Donald Trump.

"It was such a nice experience to be able to meet and talk with the president," she said. "I feel like he was very genuine in speaking with us, and we got to let him know a little bit more about Tyler and the wonderful young man that he was."

Tyler Feehan will posthumously receive the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge.

item.title: New York Islanders pick their top 8 fan-designed jerseys and social media hates them all
item.description: The New York Islanders unveiled eight finalist designs in their fan jersey design contest, but social media reaction has been overwhelmingly negative.
item.content:encoded:
Back in July, the New York Islanders announced plans to toss fans the keys and let them take a crack at designing the team's next third jersey.

I figured at the time that it would mean fans couldn't complain about this third jersey — as they did about so many jerseys the Isles have worn — if they were the ones responsible for the masterpiece or abomination.

Well, how wrong I was, because the team has unveiled the eight finalists, one of which will be selected by way of a bracket, and social media hates all the options.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

None of those are offensively awful... but none seem that exciting.

If I had to pick one because my life depended on it — and man, what a terrible stroke of luck that would be, huh? — I would probably go with the one all the way on the bottom right. Navy with the "ISLANDERS" wordmark and chest stripe.

I'm a sucker for a good ol' fashioned chest stripe.

It's kind of a shame that the Elite 8 is a little lackluster, because the design tool the team rolled out was great.

JOSH ALLEN DELIVERS FULL-THROATED UNSOLICITED DEFENSE OF BUFFALO BILLS' HIDEOUS NEW UNIFORMS

In fact, yours truly submitted at least one design that I thought was pretty great...

...their loss, I suppose.

But these all seem pretty tame, and one even looks almost exactly like the Edmonton Oilers' old orange jerseys that they used to wear.

NHL fans, many of whom likely had their designs shot down as I did, took to social media to voice their displeasure with the team's selected crop of potential sweaters.

Well, while the reception has not been warm, it looks like one of those eight sweaters will be hitting the ice.

According to the team's original release about the contest, the winner will debut next season, with the winning designer earning themselves a "VIP gameday experience."

item.title: Carville warns Democrats may need to block far-left candidates from joining caucus, moderate group disagrees
item.description: James Carville says Democratic Party leadership may need to block far-left candidates from the caucus and committees to protect the party's brand but a moderate group disagrees.
item.content:encoded:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned last week that the Democratic Party may need to consider shutting out far-left candidates in order to keep them from co-opting the party.

In recent months, several high-profile elections have seen far-left candidates, including candidates aligned with or backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, defeat their establishment opponents. Carville has warned in response that there may need to be a formal "schism" within the Democratic Party to stop it from being taken over.

Last week, "The Sharpe Exchange" podcast host Wyatt Sharpe asked Carville about whether he sees this phenomenon of anti-establishment Democrats as a growing phenomenon.

"Well, it's certainly getting more common. I mean, you can't deny that," Carville replied. "They’re very aggressive. The country overwhelmingly rejects their agenda."

JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY WILL TEST TRUE STRENGTH OF PARTY'S SOCIALIST WING

He lamented that even though many of the far-left candidates identify themselves as democratic socialists, they run in primaries as Democrats. 

"Why do you want the name Democratic? Call yourself something else. You're not you're not a Democrat! These people are not Democrats," he said. "Why not get your own name? Why do you have to appropriate our name?"

He then suggested that the Democratic Party’s leadership will need to take concrete institutional steps to protect its brand and its control of the party.

"I think that Hakeem [Jeffries] and other people are going to have to consider some of these people who run against Democrats, should they be allowed in the Democratic caucus? Should they be assigned committees, assuming that we win the House?" Carville asked.

He also wondered if there are certain politicians whom Democrats will have to tell, "‘Well, no, you can't. You're not a member of our party.’"

"At some point, it's, you know, political parties, and you can say, ‘Hey, I feel like I'm a Republican. I feel like a Democrat. I feel like I'm an independent.’ But there are people that are actually appropriating the name of the Democratic Party while they're running against the Democratic Party," Carville said. "Well, the party should be able to take some measures to protect its brand."

JEFFRIES' SOCIALISM DILEMMA: NEW YORK VICTORIES EXPOSE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DIVIDE

He listed several centrist Democrats running for office, arguing that the party of those candidates "is being hijacked" by the new faction.

The center-left think tank Third Way spoke to Fox News Digital about Carville's comments.

"If someone gets elected as a Democratic Socialist and wants to caucus as a Democrat in the House and the Senate, they should be able to do so. Let’s not forget, Bernie Sanders has never been a registered Democrat in his life, and he’s caucused as a Democrat in both the House and the Senate for more than three decades," Jim Kessler, Third Way's executive vice president for policy said. 

"Is there a line that could get you tossed out of the tent? Yes, but it has to be truly abhorrent personal behavior or taking a political position that is deeply offensive to a segment of the population," he added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Kessler shared one key warning, however, about the worst-case scenario.

"My issue with the DSA members potentially coming to the caucus is whether they are trying to hold a place in the tent or trying to burn the tent to the ground," he said. "Listening to some DSA members, they seem to be armed with a torch. Nonetheless, if they get elected fair and square, they should have their place. But only their place."

item.title: Florida man arrested doing 110 mph tells deputy he was racing to catch his cheating girlfriend
item.description: A DeSoto County Sheriff's Office deputy jailed Gavin Ames after he was clocked at 110 mph, allegedly racing to catch his cheating girlfriend.
item.content:encoded:
A deputy with the DeSoto County Sheriff's Office stood between a Florida man and his attempt to catch his cheating girlfriend in the act. To be completely fair to the officer here, he was just doing his job.

Florida's "super speeder" law put Gavin Ames in handcuffs in the back of the deputy's vehicle. He was clocked just before 1 a.m. on Aug. 1 for allegedly driving 110 mph in a 60 mph zone, FOX 13 reported.

When the deputy asked him the reason he was driving so fast, Ames didn’t dispute that he was speeding or even trying to play word games in order to search for an excuse.

FLORIDA MAN IN BUNNY HELMET ALLEGEDLY LED POLICE ON 120 MPH CHASE BEFORE SURRENDERING TO TROOPERS

He didn’t need to. He had a perfectly good excuse. Not one that was going to get him out of trouble, but one that anyone who has been cheated on can relate to.

He replied to the deputy, "I'm actually on my way to my cheating girlfriend's house." That answer was met with the customary step out of the vehicle and put your hands behind your back.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The deputy then explained that anything over 50 mph over the speed limit was good for a free trip to jail. He placed Ames in cuffs and then in his vehicle for his free trip.

Trying to process the fact that he had ended up in the back of a police vehicle while he was on his way to catch his girlfriend cheating on him brought Ames an interesting realization.

He was going to be calling this cheating girlfriend of his to bail him out.

"I’m just in shock right now. I’m in the back of a cop car listening to Boss Man D-Lo at one o’clock in the morning to catch my cheating girlfriend," Ames said on video to the deputy from the backseat of the deputy's vehicle.

"Now, I’m going to get bailed out by her." 

All in all, the early morning could have ended much worse for this Florida man. He could have caused an accident or, potentially even worse, actually caught his girlfriend in the act and snapped.

item.title: Georgia teacher, father hailed as hero after dying to save girl from Myrtle Beach rip current
item.description: Derrick Moore, a Georgia teacher and father of four, rescued a stranger's child from a rip current off Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, before vanishing.
item.content:encoded:
A beloved Georgia elementary school teacher and father died after jumping into the ocean to save a young girl caught in a rip current off Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, according to authorities and his family.

Derrick Moore, 47, entered the water near 10th Avenue South after a young girl became caught in a rip current at approximately 7:53 p.m. Friday, according to the Myrtle Beach Police Department.

Moore was able to get the girl to safety but was then pulled underwater by the rip current and disappeared, police said. The incident occurred after lifeguards had gone off duty.

MAN, WOMAN KILLED IN RIP CURRENT AS LIFEGUARD SHORTAGE LEAVES DANGER ZONES IN BEACH DESTINATION

Myrtle Beach police and firefighters continued searching for Moore into Saturday morning. Police announced Saturday afternoon that his body had washed ashore and was recovered.

Moore's daughter told WRAL that her father did not know the girl he risked his life to save.

"We loved him and are truly heartbroken that he's gone," his daughter said in a statement to the outlet. "He was a great father and we are all going to miss him."

Moore leaves behind four children, according to a GoFundMe page.

As news of his death spread, tributes poured in from Moore's friends, former teammates and family members, who remembered him as a devoted father, gifted athlete and selfless man whose final act reflected the way he lived his life.

HEROIC 16-YEAR-OLD LIFEGUARD RESCUES CHILD FROM MONSTER SURF IN HEART-STOPPING VIDEO

The DeKalb County School District confirmed Moore was a current teacher at Rockbridge Elementary School in Georgia, where his students affectionately referred to him as "Coach." He previously taught at Jolly Elementary School.

"The DeKalb County School District is deeply saddened by the passing of Mr. Derrick Moore, a beloved educator and valued member of the DeKalb County School District (DCSD) family," the district said in a statement.

The district said Moore "made a meaningful impact on the students, families, colleagues, and communities he served," adding that his "presence, care, and dedication to education will be deeply missed."

Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also paid tribute to Moore.

"Marty and I were heartbroken to learn of the tragic loss of Derrick Moore, a father, teacher, and coach," Kemp said. "Please join us in praying for this hero’s family and the DeKalb County community as they mourn his loss."

LIFEGUARDS SAVE YOUNG BOY, 5 YEARS OLD, AS HE'S PULLED UNCONSCIOUS FROM OCEAN

Moore was also remembered as a standout athlete whose ties to sports stretched back to his college years.

Samford University said Moore graduated in 2001 and competed in both football and track and field.

"The Samford community mourns the loss of alumnus Derrick Moore, who tragically passed after rescuing a girl struggling in a rip current in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina," the university said in a statement.

The university remembered Moore as a "beloved teacher" and "true hero" and asked the Samford community to keep his family in their prayers.

Friends and former teammates also remembered Moore as someone who showed up for others, with one writing that the fact he gave his life trying to save someone else "tells you everything you need to know about the kind of man he was."

Family members echoed that sentiment, sharing memories of Moore as a devoted father, son and brother who made a point of being present for the people he loved.

One family member described Moore's decision to enter the water to save a child he did not know as a fitting final example of his selflessness.

"You died a HERO. You died saving the life of a child, a stranger. What a Legacy," the family member wrote.

item.title: Riley Green shares how Luke Grimes unexpectedly launched his acting career, reveals job he left behind
item.description: Riley Green reveals how Luke Grimes encouraged him to audition for "Marshals," helping the country star land his first acting role as a Navy SEAL.
item.content:encoded:
Riley Green may be one of country music’s rising stars, but his latest on-screen career move came with a little help from a famous friend.

During an appearance on "CBS Mornings" on Monday, the 37-year-old Alabama native revealed that "Yellowstone" star Luke Grimes helped open the door to his first acting role, encouraging Green to step outside his comfort zone and eventually helping land him a part on the CBS drama "Marshals."

"It happened so organically because he was starting his music career and coming to Nashville a little bit. We wrote together," said Green, who made his acting debut as Garrett — a former Navy SEAL struggling with PTSD — alongside Grimes in the "Yellowstone" spinoff.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN SHOCKS 'YELLOWSTONE' FANS WITH NEW SPINOFF SERIES, PROVIDES VIEWERS WITH DARK RIDE

"He mentioned something about maybe I should act. I said, 'Well I'm interested.' He said, 'I've got this show.' A couple months later, I went out and read for a part. They said I got it. I flew back out to Utah and we filmed the show."

Earlier this year, Green admitted it's not every day an opportunity like that presents itself.

"I guess that doesn't happen all the time, where the star of the show sits in with somebody trying out for a part," Green told USA Today. "But man, I've got to be such good friends with Luke, and it makes it so much easier to step into a world that I wasn't necessarily comfortable in."

It was a dramatic change for a performer accustomed to playing sold-out concerts.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN’S 'YELLOWSTONE’ FORMULA TURNS COUNTRY STARS INTO SCENE-STEALERS AS MORGAN WADE MAKES HER DEBUT

Green previously admitted acting was considerably more intimidating than taking the stage.

"I don’t get nervous going on stage anymore," Green previously told Fox News Digital at the "Marshals" premiere. "I’ve played enough shows now it kind of comes naturally, but this was a completely different world, and it’s not my set, it’s not my stage."

His Hollywood debut was the latest unexpected chapter in a career Green never necessarily envisioned for himself.

Long before he found fame, Green was earning his living as a construction worker, framing homes until he signed a record deal in 2018.

LAINEY WILSON SAYS CITY PEOPLE HAVE WRONG VIEW OF COUNTRY TOWNS AS SHE DEFENDS HER 'BLUE COLLAR' ROOTS

And according to Green, he wouldn't have been able to handle the spotlight at the time.

Advertisement

"I've been so fortunate that my success was gradual," he told the CBS hosts. "Early 20s, I don't know if I could have handled what I've got going on right now, but it's been really motivating. I've done it for well over 10 years now."

"I was building houses for a living. And I signed a record deal in 2018 and put my tool belt up and really went on the road heavy and it's just, as a songwriter, it's so great when people are like relating to the music, and you hear them singing those songs back to you."

"When you see it growing, it just makes you want to go play more shows and keep grinding," he continued. "So it's a really great time to be in country music because I think the genre as a whole is becoming more popular everywhere."

COUNTRY STAR RILEY GREEN REVEALS WHY FAN EMOTION AT HIS SHOWS BEATS INDUSTRY AWARDS EVERY TIME

Green signed with Big Machine Label Group in 2018 and broke through with "There Was This Girl," followed by hits including "I Wish Grandpas Never Died," "Half of Me," "Different 'Round Here," "You Look Like You Love Me" with Ella Langley and "Worst Way."

Yet despite his success — and his unexpected entry into Hollywood — Green has remained closely tied to the life he had before fame.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He continues to live on his farm in Alabama rather than relocating full-time to Nashville.

"I feel like I’ve got every reason in the world to move to Nashville, and it’s just never crossed my mind," Green previously told Fox News Digital.

"Me in real life, I'd rather be on my bulldozer on a farm, or hunting somewhere."

item.title: Man, 20, dies in 'horrific accident' after slipping from towering Oregon waterfall
item.description: The visitor reportedly ventured off-trail near the top of South Falls at the Silver Falls State Park in Oregon before plunging into the water roughly 177 feet below.
item.content:encoded:
A 20-year-old male hiker reportedly died Monday in what park officials described as a "horrific accident" following a devastating fall from a 177-foot waterfall at an Oregon state park.

Authorities said the man was from out of state and was visiting Silver Falls State Park, more than an hour south of Portland, according to Central Oregon Daily.

The visitor reportedly went off-trail while trying to reach an area where he could pose for a photo, crossing a barrier and making his way over a creek directly above the falls.

The incident happened at the upper viewpoint of South Falls, the park’s tallest waterfall, which cascades into a large pool below, Oregon State Police said, according to the outlet.

NPS INVESTIGATES AFTER 23-YEAR-OLD REPORTEDLY SWEPT OVER NOTORIOUS YOSEMITE WATERFALL

He then fell into the pool below at around 6:30 p.m.

Bystanders at the park reportedly tried to help, performing CPR as emergency responders rushed to the scene.

The victim died at the scene, according to KPTV. Authorities did not release his identity.

RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION

"It was a pretty horrific accident," Silver Falls State Park regional manager Chris Gilliand said, according to Central Oregon Daily. "A very tough situation."

The Marion County Medical Examiner reportedly released the man's body to Marion County Search and Rescue.

Search and rescue personnel then completed the recovery from the base of the falls.

Unger Funeral Chapel later took custody, according to reports.

Silver Falls State Park is known for its Trail of Ten Falls, a popular hiking route featuring 10 waterfalls and attracting visitors from across Oregon and beyond.

South Falls is considered one of the park's main attractions and features a trail that allows visitors to walk behind the waterfall. The waterfall has been described as the "crown jewel" of Oregon's state parks.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Oregon State Police and Silver Falls State Park for more information.

item.title: Zac Taylor admits breaking NFL challenge flag rule for 8 years as league makes change
item.description: Taylor usually gave the red challenge flag to another staff member, which is now allowed following the NFL's rule change before the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
A slight change to an NFL rule has been set before the start of the 2026 season, but it’s nothing new for Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor.

He admitted he’s technically been breaking an NFL rule for the past eight years.

The change is that each team’s head coach will be able to delegate the ability to use the red challenge flag to someone else on the staff if they so wish.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

It was the responsibility of the head coach to challenge a play, throwing the red flag on the field for review.

Now, the head coach has the ability to name a pregame challenge designee that will be responsible for those moments during the game.

VIKINGS QUARTERBACK BATTLE MEETS EXPECTED END AS KYLER MURRAY BEATS OUT JJ MCCARTHY FOR STARTING JOB

But in 2019, when Taylor was named the Bengals’ head coach, he wasn’t the one holding the flag. It was Doug Rosfeld, his chief of coaching staff, throwing the flag instead.

That’s the way Taylor has been running that aspect of his many duties as head coach, which he revealed on Tuesday during his press conference.

"We’ve been breaking that rule for eight years because I’ve never thrown a challenge flag," he said.

Taylor even added that he’d let referees know he wasn’t the one throwing it before the game, and they never took an issue with Rosfeld having that duty.

"They ask you that in pregame, who’s got the flag," Taylor mentioned. "It’s never been an issue. I didn’t even know it was frowned upon. I know there’s other coaches in the league, I’m not the only one who’s done that. I saw they implemented a new rule, so maybe we’ll get a retroactive fine or something."

Many coaches are creatures of habit so, despite the rule change, those that have the red challenge flag on their person during games will likely keep it that way. Some leave it in their pant pockets, while some even have it tucked into their socks (Bill Belichick’s favorite spot).

For Taylor, he said "it’s easier for me" not to have the flag on him during the game. One of the reasons is due to the ending of an offensive series, which he does the play-calling for, where he’ll immediately go talk to his players.

In that time, if there is a challengeable play, Rosfeld will be the one watching and determining whether it’s worth throwing the flag.

Every team, every coach works different from each other. But this slight rule change is something Taylor isn’t even batting an eye at.

He’s been handling it that way the entire time.

"They always made it clear to me that I have to be next to Doug," Taylor added. item.title: At every opportunity, Anthony Fauci hid the truth about COVID, masks, from the American public
item.description: A newly released email shows Anthony Fauci knew about asymptomatic transmission months before he cited it as his reason to reverse mask guidance.
item.content:encoded:
Six and a half years after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and after years of most in the media and the political class pretending it never happened, our response to the spread of the coronavirus is back in the news. All thanks to the not-so-fearless leader of our pandemic policy making, former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases head Anthony Fauci.

Fauci spent years, starting in early 2020 and beyond, as the center of attention in the United States and beyond. And boy did he know it and revel in it. Promoted by the media as a star "expert," an unbiased keeper of all scientific knowledge, and made into a celebrity thanks to his obvious political leanings and anti-Trump messaging, Fauci became beloved. Just ask him.

The release of his diaries though, revealed some thoroughly discrediting and upsetting details about Fauci's private beliefs.

ANTHONY FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY AND EMAILS SHOW HE KNEW LOCKDOWNS FAILED AND PUSHED MASKS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

He knew that lockdowns weren't working, saying that cases seemed to rise and fall regardless of what was closed and when. He knew that there was no justification for masking other than "everyone else is doing it already," and a desire to fit in with the CDC. He knew that COVID-19 vaccines weren't stopping the spread, and even worried about getting infected at an event that required proof of vaccination to attend. He was in communication with important media figures like CNN's Jake Tapper or Dana Bash, or in Tapper's case, described a budding friendship and dinner parties during the early part of the pandemic.

But it's not just his diaries. We now have some texts, released by Sen. Ron Johnson, that indicate he was privately concerned about COVID-19 vaccine side effects and thought they were worth investigating. And alerting his partners in the Biden administration, who concurred.

In one already-infamous newly released text, Fauci said that the COVID-19 vaccine "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester."

Sen. Rand Paul, one of Fauci's harshest government critics, addressed that new release in a post on X.

"Once again, Anthony Fauci was saying one thing in public and something completely different in private," he said. "He was willing to put women and their unborn children at risk instead of admitting that he was wrong about the vaccines that he tried guilting Americans into taking."

But even that buries the lede: not only was Fauci saying something different in public and private, he went on television, with his buddies, and described anyone who raised such concerns as dangerous conspiracy theorists.

Thus far, there isn't a lot of high-quality evidence that the COVID-19 vaccine is associated with increased risk of miscarriage. Despite some big numbers being floated around on social media, most research has not found an elevated risk relative to normal rates. That's not the point though. The point is that nobody was allowed to talk about it.

When you limit conversation, when you make public statements of confirmation that everything's safe, effective, and there's nothing to see here, you risk losing trust if there is a legitimate concern to investigate. And there were legitimate concerns, even if not about miscarriages.

NBA STAR KYRIE IRVING GOT HIS APOLOGY, BUT FOUR COVID-ERA ATHLETES STILL WAITING FOR THEIRS FROM THE MEDIA

Myocarditis was ignored, downplayed, or ultimately dismissed. There were side effects that affected significant numbers of people. Fauci, clearly, privately believed that some of these issues necessitated investigation. While publicly saying something completely different, and implying the public shouldn't even be able to have those concerns or discussions.

Importantly, it wasn't just vaccine side effects that was dishonest about. And one of his emails undermines his later messaging on masking too.

When Fauci joined 60 Minutes in February 2020, he specifically stated that there was "no reason to be walking around with a mask."

Even more importantly, he said that masks do not provide the type of protection people think they do, that they might block a droplet or two, but could even backfire since people touch their faces more when wearing a mask.

That was all true and correct. Masks don't work, they don't provide protection, they do touch their face more frequently, and nobody needed to wear them. Obviously, however, Fauci changed his story months later. Masks become the single most important thing you could do, to the point where "wear a mask" became one of the most important phrases of 2020, according to CBS at the time.

Yet in a rare instance of even moderately difficult questioning posed to the saint-like Fauci, when asked about later, he defended his flip flop by saying he was lying to protect supply for healthcare workers. And didn't know about asymptomatic COVID-19 spread at the time.

"I don't regret anything I said then because in the context of the time in which I said it, it was correct. We were told in our task force meetings that we have a serious problem with the lack of PPEs and masks for the health providers who are putting themselves in harm's way every day to take care of sick people," Fauci said in an interview with Norah O'Donnell.

"When it became clear that the infection could be spread by asymptomatic carriers who don't know they're infected, that made it very clear that we had to strongly recommend masks," he added.

Putting aside that it's a monumental lie to claim that health providers would order PPE and masks from Amazon, like the public, and that cloth masks are not what health providers use, it's revealing that he claims his flip flop in April 2020 was based on learning about asymptomatic spread.

Except, that's also a lie. And we know it, because of what Fauci wrote in an email.

On January 30, 2020, Fauci wrote, "Another amazing and difficult day." He went on to describe what he'd learned about the spread of the virus, including this important note:

"Mart Cetron who was listening in on the WHO call said that the epidemic was accelerating that this is was clear that the incubation period was shorter (2-5 days than was previously felt and that asymptomatic transmission was occurring.)"

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Ah. Interesting. So in January 2020, Fauci knew that asymptomatic transmission was happening, because he'd been told that by someone listening in on a call with the World Health Organization. In February 2020, he went on 60 Minutes and said that nobody needed to wear masks because they don't work. In April 2020, he changed his mind and says everyone should be wearing masks. Then later in 2020, he tells CBS that he changed his mind on recommending masks because of asymptomatic transmission.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK CULTURE COVERAGE

Spectacular, historic, inexcusable dishonesty. He knew in January that asymptomatic spread was happening. He still said masks didn't work and weren't necessarily the following month. Then when asked to justify his change of heart, he lies again and says it's because he learned about asymptomatic spread, after telling the public not to wear masks. A malicious, vindictive, prolific series of lies.

As always, the more we learn about Anthony Fauci, the worse he looks. His primary goal wasn't serving and helping the public, or accurately communicating risks, trade-offs, or uncertainty. It was promoting himself and misleading Americans to service his own agenda. That's his real legacy, and why trust in public health has never been lower.

item.title: Bella Thorne says Hollywood treated her like a kid on screen and an adult off camera
item.description: Bella Thorne opens up about the moment she turned 18 and finally felt free after years of navigating Hollywood's impossible child star expectations.
item.content:encoded:
Bella Thorne's life as a child star came with a harsh reality: Hollywood expected her to be a kid on screen and an adult everywhere else.

Thorne began working in entertainment as a child, appearing as a model before taking on television roles in shows including HBO’s "Big Love." Her major breakthrough arrived in 2010 when she was cast as CeCe Jones opposite Zendaya’s Rocky Blue in Disney Channel’s "Shake It Up."

"You're ... spending all of your hours a day on set with adults, you know, that is – it's like such a different, the brain's like how do I–" Thorne explained during an appearance on "Call Her Daddy."

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

"And I'm expected to be this child, but I'm also working like hours like an adult and being in adult conversations," she added. "And when I f--k up it's my bad, not like a child – It's my bad. Like you're an adult, it's your bad."

But navigating those adult expectations while growing up in the public eye didn't come easily for Thorne.

"Well, I think people can see how I've managed it publicly," she told host Alexandra Cooper. "They can see it, they've got photos of it. Oh, they got all the photos. Oh, wow. I don't know that I ever handled it or balanced it out correctly."

"I don't think that I ever had that mental clarity," Thorne acknowledged. "I've worked a lot on the more recent side. I got to a point where I just needed to kind of change things in my life and get better at – I was working so much and yet was leaving very little time for the things that I really, really cared about."

FORMER DISNEY STAR MAITLAND WARD SAYS YOUNG ACTORS WERE TREATED LIKE A 'PRODUCT' IN HOLLYWOOD FACTORY

Thorne said she spent the past two years working to prioritize her mental health, a shift that became especially important after "Color Your Hurt" left her feeling emotionally drained. The now 28-year-old actress revealed she finally gave herself "some space to breathe" along with grace.

"I don't think I ever did that when I was younger," she said.

While Thorne struggled to give herself that same grace as a child star, she recalled feeling a dramatic shift when she turned 18.

"...I was like, 'I'm free,'" the "Midnight Sun" star recalled.

"Like I'm literally free. Like I'm walking into this house and no one's asking me when I'm like, when I'm gonna be there, when this time or when I'm gonna leave. It ... was such a weird – and you don't know what's weird until someone else tells you it's weird."

Thorne also spoke candidly about being compared to her fellow Disney Channel stars, including Selena Gomez, Miley Cyrus and Demi Lovato.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I didn't so much hang out with people from the network," Thorne recalled. "I hung out with Zendaya, we hung out ... 'Shake It Up' was in a different time when Miley and Selena and Demi and those shows – They were all, I think 16, 17 when we were starting. So the eras are so different, and yet they intersect."

She said people questioned whether she would become Disney's next "bad girl," something she struggled to comprehend at such a young age.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"And I remember when I was 12, people asking me if I was gonna be – comparing us all, all the Disney girls and with Miley and Selena and this new era – and asking which was gonna be the next bad girl," Thorne claimed. "And, 'Are you gonna be like Lindsay Lohan?' And like all these things at 12, 13 – you're just, your brain is like trying so hard. 'Like am I gonna be like what? Like what? What is the question?' Like, oh my God."

Thorne later moved beyond her Disney image with a steady mix of film and television roles.

Thorne has also made a bigger push behind the camera. In August 2026, she signed on to write, direct and star in "Spring Breakers 2," following her feature directorial debut, "Color Your Hurt."

item.title: Trump's Justice Department sues New York, other blue states over tuition for illegal immigrants
item.description: Trump's DOJ filed lawsuits against New York, Connecticut, and Vermont over laws it claims provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to illegal immigrants.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Justice under the Trump administration announced Monday that it plans to file lawsuits against New York, Connecticut and Vermont over laws that it claims provide in-state tuition and other financial incentives to illegal immigrants.

"These laws unconstitutionally discriminate against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rates or scholarships, create incentives for illegal immigration, and reward illegal aliens with benefits that U.S. citizens are not eligible for, all in direct conflict with federal law," a statement from the department read.

According to the legal complaints, the Department of Justice is seeking to enjoin enforcement of laws that provide financial assistance to illegal immigrants or provide tuition rates to any immigrants "who maintain in-state residency, regardless of whether they are lawfully present."

NEBRASKA ENDS IN-STATE TUITION BENEFITS FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER DOJ DEAL

"This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in a press release. "This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, the Department of Justice expressed confidence in its latest lawsuits, boasting legal wins in five other states with similar complaints.

"Under the leadership of Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department’s efforts have already delivered wins for the American people, as five similar lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois have resulted favorable orders permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional analogous laws that gave reduced tuition to illegal aliens, including an order from the Fifth Circuit," the statement read.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong pushed back on the lawsuit against his state in a comment to Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

OVER 100 CALIFORNIA COLLEGES ACCUSED OF DISCRIMINATING AGAINST US-BORN STUDENTS IN NEW DOJ COMPLAINT

"Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut. How we run our schools and teach our kids is none of your business, and you have no authority to force the sovereign state of Connecticut to deny our kids a future," Tong said. "I fought for this bill as a legislator when it passed in 2011, and I’ll fight to defend Connecticut families now from this cruel attack. Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start."

Fox News Digital also reached out to New York and Vermont's attorneys general for comment on the developing lawsuits.

As of Monday, the Department of Justice has filed 17 lawsuits targeting laws that the Trump administration has claimed provide reduced tuition for illegal immigrants. The other states sued included Minnesota, Virginia, California, New Jersey, Kansas, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland and Colorado.

FLORIDA BOARD VOTES TO BAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM PUBLIC COLLEGE ADMISSIONS

Last month, a federal judge provided a win for the Trump administration's Justice Department after ruling that Illinois' in-state tuition policies, the RISE Act and the Illinois DREAM Act, were "unconstitutional and invalid." The department originally sued Illinois in September 2025.

item.title: Trump directs CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz to end Medicaid gender transition funding for minors
item.description: Trump instructed CMS to end Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures, calling the surgeries "barbaric" in a Truth Social post.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration will no longer fund gender transition surgeries using Medicaid for minors, President Donald Trump said Tuesday, calling such procedures "barbaric."

In a Truth Social post, Trump said he ordered Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, to stop using the joint federal and state public health insurance program to fund such procedures.

"We are not going to pay for our innocent children to undergo these barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies," Trump wrote.

SEN HAWLEY WARNS IT WOULD BE 'UNCONSCIONABLE' IF BILLIONS OF TAXPAYER FUNDS FLOW TO TRANS KIDS’ SEX CHANGES

Trump's announcement came after CMS said it would begin implementing a rule that ends the use of federal Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) funding for gender-affirming care for children and youth.

That includes puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and surgical operations, which "can result in irreversible damage, including infertility, impaired sexual function, diminished bone density, altered brain development, and other lasting physiological effects."

"Children deserve our protection, not experimental interventions that pose serious risks and convey no proven benefits," Oz said in a statement. "By cutting off federal funds for these sex-rejecting procedures, we’re following the science, saving taxpayer dollars, and, most importantly, protecting children from potentially irreversible harm so they can truly flourish."

The rule is slated to take effect on Oct. 13. It does not affect coverage of mental health services.

COLORADO SUPREME COURT ORDERS CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TO RESUME GENDER TRANSITION TREATMENTS FOR MINORS

The move by the CMS follows a Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) review of national and international research. The review found "significant evidence gaps, documented serious safety concerns, and concluded that the evidence supporting these interventions for children remains insufficient to justify federal taxpayer funding."

The CMS pointed to the United Kingdom's Cass Review as one of the cornerstone pieces of research informing the decision.

That review, conducted by Dr. Hilary Cass, concluded in 2024 that research on medical interventions like cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers was limited and not definitive. The report also said that medical interventions had developed significantly faster than evidence proving those interventions were safe.

"The Trump Administration is drawing a clear line: America’s children will not be subjected to life-altering interventions on the taxpayer’s dime without reliable evidence of safety and clinical benefit," HHS Press Secretary Emily Hilliard told Fox News Digital.

"Under the leadership of Secretary Kennedy, federal health care dollars will support evidence-based care that protects children and puts their long-term health first," she added. "American taxpayers should never be forced to finance interventions when the evidence of benefit is insufficient and the potential consequences for children can be serious and irreversible."

Twenty-seven states have enacted restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors, according to KFF, a health policy group.

Republican lawmakers have moved to restrict such procedures for minors, while many Democrats have said such restrictions are attacks against trans people.

In his Truth Social post, Trump said many hospitals across the country have ended such "gender-affirming care," with many more expected to follow.

"Just think about all of the young, innocent, and perhaps confused children who will be spared!" he wrote. "While the Democrat Party wants your kids to be able to chop off their reproductive organs before they are old enough to vote."

He also urged his followers to remember the Democratic Party's position on the matter ahead of November's midterm elections.

item.title: A combination of bad coaching hires and subpar quarterback play is the culprit for SEC's recent swoon
item.description: SEC football hasn't won a national championship in three years despite adding Oklahoma and Texas, and coaching hires may be the biggest reason why.
item.content:encoded:
It has been a hotly debated topic in college football circles as to whether the SEC's reign of dominance has ended after a nearly 20-year run, and while I'm not here to bury the league just yet, it's hard to argue they've taken a step back.

From 2006 to 2023, an SEC team won a staggering 13 of a possible 17 national championships during the era of both the BCS and College Football Playoff.

However, the once-dominant Southeastern Conference hasn't won a championship in three years despite adding two traditional powers to its ranks (Oklahoma and Texas) and hasn't even reached the title game since Georgia won it all in January 2023.

PERCEPTION IS REALITY, AND THE SEC NEEDS TO START WINNING AGAIN BEFORE IT CONTINUES TO PUFF OUT ITS CHEST

Many people like to point to the advents of NIL and the transfer portal as the boogie men responsible for the SEC's downfall, but to me, it's a far more nuanced conversation than just saying "paying players is legal now, therefore the SEC sucks."

While there may not be a single issue that is easily identifiable, I can think of two reasons as to why the SEC has experienced its recent CFP swoon.

First, and perhaps most importantly, the coaching hires at several top-flight SEC programs have left much to be desired.

Some coaching changes were flat out downgrades from their predecessors while others, while not necessarily poor coaches in their own right, were terrible fits and never should have been considered in the first place.

Let's start with the two tentpole programs of the conference since the league went to a championship game format, Alabama and Florida.

Since the SEC expanded to 12 teams in 1992 and implemented the SEC Championship Game, both the Tide and Gators are first and second in league titles, with 11 and seven, respectively.

When the conference was in its early stages of ascending to dominance in the late 2000s, two of the greatest coaches of their era called Tuscaloosa and Gainesville home.

Nick Saban won six national championships while coaching the Crimson Tide, but when he called it quits in 2024, Alabama needed to find someone to fill his shoes.

Enter Kalen DeBoer.

DID ALABAMA DOOM THEMSELVES TO MEDIOCRITY WITH KALEN DEBOER EXTENSION?

Now, DeBoer isn't a bad coach, per se, but he isn't Saban, and Bama has failed to live up to its legendary status from the decade prior since he arrived.

For the Gators, it's been way worse since Urban Meyer left.

A program like Florida, with all its resources and in-state talent available, should never bottom out like it did in 2025, but the crazy thing is they've experienced three separate four-win seasons since the legendary coach Meyer walked out the door in 2010.

A run of subpar coaching hires culminated in the Billy Napier tenure, who was, by every metric, the worst coach in Gator football history since World War II.

His arrival coincided with the steady decline of the SEC starting with the 2023 season, and although Florida wasn't a perennial contender from 2010-2022 before hiring Napier, his destruction of the program has left a void where a once-proud national power used to be.

For another SEC powerhouse in LSU, it's a bit more complex.

If we are talking purely from an X's and O's standpoint, I believe Brian Kelly is a better coach than former Tigers head man Ed Orgeron, so I understood and even joined in the optimism for the Bayou Bengals when they hired the former to replace the latter in November 2021.

BY ADDING ED ORGERON TO STAFF, LANE KIFFIN AND LSU ADDRESS KEY FLAW FROM PREVIOUS REGIME

Coach O had won a national title while in Baton Rouge, so surely Kelly could do the same, right?

There are two main differences separating Kelly and Orgeron that made one more successful than the other: willingness to delegate and culture fit.

The culture fit piece is perhaps more nebulous but equally important, and while Orgeron fit LSU like a glove, Kelly stuck out like a sore thumb.

Kelly's inability or unwillingness to accept the "LSU way" doomed him from day one, and it's a big reason he was ousted as unceremoniously as he was while Coach O has been welcomed back with open arms.

What Orgeron lacked in game-day coaching acumen he more than made up for in recognizing talent and delegating, both on the field and with his coaches.

Having Dave Aranda and Joe Brady (along with Steve Ensminger) orchestrating the Tigers' defense and offense, respectively, led to the record-breaking 2019 season that saw quarterback Joe Burrow win a Heisman and guide LSU to a historic national championship.

Speaking of Burrow, let's transition to the other half of the equation regarding the SEC's steady decline.

Talent has started to equalize at the top, particularly between the SEC and Big Ten, and when talent is equal, coaching and quarterback play act as the tiebreaker.

We touched on coaching, but what about quarterback play?

There's no question that when the SEC was ripping off their run of national championships that the quarterbacks were outrageously talented.

Players like Tim Tebow, Cam Newton, Tua Tagovailoa, the aforementioned Burrow, and even a guy like Mac Jones were all Heisman winners or finalists who elevated the play of the team around them and ultimately captured college football's biggest prize.

Since the Big Ten started their own run of dominance in the sport, the balance of power under center has shifted heavily away from the SEC.

Even during Georgia's run of back-to-back national championships in 2021 and 2022, the Dawgs had a player like Stetson Bennett, a Heisman finalist in his own right whose stats were otherworldly despite his relative obscurity and circuitous path to becoming a starting QB.

It's not like the SEC has missed out on talented signal-callers, but it seems like all the best quarterbacks are playing for the lower-level teams in the league that have no shot at winning the title.

Hopefully for the league's sake, that changes this year with players like Arch Manning and Trinidad Chambliss leading Playoff-caliber teams near the top of the league, but it seems like whenever the league gets a quarterback that is capable of winning a championship, he ends up on either a flawed team like Jayden Daniels with LSU in 2023 or a team that just isn't talented enough like Diego Pavia on last year's Vanderbilt team.

Sometimes, transcendent quarterback play can even lift a mediocre coach to glory, as we saw with Cam Newton at Auburn in 2010.

With all due respect to Gene Chizik, he had no business winning a national championship, especially with that 2010 Auburn team, but Newton's superhero performance that season elevated them to a dream ending.

Obviously, there are way more factors that go into the shift of the balance of power in college football, and these theories are neither exhaustive nor foolproof, but they're a good start and way more in depth and nuanced than just pointing at NIL and the transfer portal.

The SEC still has the talent for a team from its ranks to win it all, and there are still plenty of great coaches and quarterbacks within the Southeastern Conference to perhaps break the drought in 2026.

Coaches like Kirby Smart, Lane Kiffin, and Steve Sarkisian have the chops to make a run this season and will have great teams with talented, veteran quarterbacks to boot.

Whether they put it all together or cede to the Big Ten once again remains to be seen, but I think I speak for everyone when I say I can't wait to see how it all plays out.

item.title: Kaia Gerber owns 'nepo baby' status while questioning other celebrity kids: 'Show me why you deserve this job'
item.description: Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere tackle the nepo baby debate in Vogue's September cover story as they star together in Ryan Murphy's FX series "The Shards."
item.content:encoded:
Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere are confronting Hollywood’s "nepo baby" debate head-on.

In Vogue’s September 2026 cover story, Gerber, daughter of supermodel Cindy Crawford, and Gere, son of Hollywood star Richard Gere opened up about the scrutiny surrounding their careers as they step into the spotlight together in Ryan Murphy’s FX series "The Shards" and acknowledged that audiences may be quick to judge them because of their famous families.

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

"I’ve only ever been a nepo baby, and I’ve only ever benefited in my career from it," Gerber, 24, told Vogue.

The model and actress admitted she can even be skeptical of other celebrity children herself, wondering whether they have earned the opportunities they receive.

"Okay, show me why you deserve this job."

Gerber said she warned her 26-year-old co-star that audiences likely wouldn't view him the same way they would an unknown actor making his debut.

CHARLIZE THERON SAYS HER KIDS WON’T GET A FREE RIDE IN HOLLYWOOD: THEY NEED TO ‘EARN IT’

"Unfortunately with this show, it’s not like you’re just any unknown actor and people will judge you as an unknown actor," she recalled telling him, adding that the scrutiny has made her "want to work harder."

Gerber began modeling as a child and has since branched into acting, including multiple projects with Murphy.

Gere took a different route into show business.

Despite growing up with an A-list father, he said he was raised largely outside Hollywood and had never stepped onto a professional set until last year.

SHARON STONE SAYS 'EUPHORIA' SHOULD BE SHOWN IN 'EVERY HIGH SCHOOL' AND REQUIRED VIEWING FOR PARENTS

Initially, Gere brushed off suggestions that he might follow in his parents’ footsteps and studied visual arts at Brown University before becoming involved in student filmmaking.

It wasn't until a talent manager saw one of his student films, that his acting career really began. He later auditioned for both "The Shards" and HBO’s "Euphoria," landing roles in each.

Gere acknowledged that his family name inevitably complicates perceptions of his success.

"I’m a very self-critical guy who would like to believe that my career’s going well for all the wrong reasons," he told Vogue, adding that continued success has made that increasingly difficult for him to believe.

MAYA HAWKE SAYS MOM UMA THURMAN PRACTICED 'WITCH-ADJACENT' REMEDIES

The casting of Gerber and Gere carries an additional Hollywood twist.

Crawford and Richard Gere were married from 1991 to 1995 and famously appeared together on the cover of Vogue in 1992. More than three decades later, their children now share the magazine’s September cover while starring opposite each other in "The Shards."

For Gerber, however, escaping comparisons to her famous mother — and assumptions about how she landed her career — may prove impossible.

Rather than run from the "nepo baby" conversation, she appears determined to let the work make her case.

item.title: Rosie O'Donnell credits Trump for making her 're-famous' as White House calls her 'obsessed'
item.description: Rosie O'Donnell told Amy Poehler that President Trump unknowingly boosted her career, calling him "Mango Mussolini" as the White House calls her "obsessed."
item.content:encoded:
Rosie O'Donnell credited President Donald Trump for her re-discovered fame on Tuesday as the White House continued to call the actress and former co-host of "The View" "obsessed."

"I feel like recently I'm re-famous. That's what I feel. I told my kids, well kids, hold on 'cause mommy's re-famous. I don't know how it happened. I think it's Mango Mussolini," O'Donnell told "Good Hang" host Amy Poehler, referring to Trump. "I think it's him who did it. He didn't know. If he knew how much he was helping my career and my life, he would shut up about me because, you know, he's a horrible creature."

O'Donnell and the president have traded barbs over the years, as the comedian remains one of Trump's fiercest critics. She moved to Ireland after Trump's 2024 election victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

JIMMY KIMMEL REVEALS HE ASKED MAJOR TRUMP CRITIC TO GUEST HOST WHILE HE'S ON VACATION AS A 'SPECIAL TREAT'

The comedian has appeared on multiple podcasts and shows, and she is set to guest host Jimmy Kimmel's show for a week beginning next week.

The White House pointed Fox News Digital to one of Trump's Truth Social posts from June 6.

The post shows four images of O'Donnell with Trump appearing in thought bubbles near her head. The caption says O'Donnell "is obsessed."

O'Donnell recently claimed that she and Trump's decades-long feud has gone on in part because of their shared roots.

ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS

"There have been so many comedians who have said things about him, but I am from the same area that he’s from," she told Variety in July.

She and Trump were born and raised in New York, and O'Donnell said that people occasionally tell her that they sound alike, "which is probably the worst thing that you can say to me."

"But I think I’m one of those tough girls from elementary school and junior high that said to him, 'Shut the hell up! You’re not playing with us. Get out of here, you freakin’ idiot!' And he never got past it. I think I trigger him like a PTSD response of all his failures in his life as a kid."

She theorized that she reminds Trump "of the girls who said, 'You're nothing,' and it scares him."

O'Donnell made similar comments this week on Sophia Bush's "Work in Progress" podcast. When Bush said that Trump is "obsessed" with her, she agreed and said Trump "grew up with girls like me — tough, probably gay Irish girls who didn't take s--- from no stupid rich boy wannabe."

O'Donnell also signaled she would be returning to ABC's "The View" for a 30th anniversary episode in the upcoming season after detailing a tense moment with host and moderator Whoopi Goldberg.
